sections.label: Viruttam (விருத்தம்)   Ragam: Bhoopalam
sections.ta:
சதுர் மறை நாயகன் சங்கரி பாலன்
சமரினில் வித்தகன் சதாசிவ நேயன்
சர்வமும் சமம் என நோக்கிடும் செங்கோலன்
சகல பாப நாசகன் சரண் எனில் அரண் அவன்
sections.translit:
chathur maRai nAyakan sankari bAlan
samarinil vitthagan sadhAsiva nEyan
sarvamum samam ena nOkkidum sengkOlan
sakala pApa nAsakan saraN enil araN avan
sections.en: He is the ruler of four vedas or scriptures, son of Goddess Sankari. Expert in warfare; adores Lord Sadhasiva. Everything is looked at as equal in his kingdom. Destroyer of every evil deed; he becomes a fortress with just the utterance of surrender.

sections.label: Pallavi
sections.ta:
சங்கரன் மைந்தனே சங்கடம் களைவோனே
ஐங்கர வேந்தனே வந்தருள் தந்திடுக
sections.translit:
sankaran maindhanE sankatam kaLaivOnE
aingkara vEndhanE vandharuL thandhiduga
sections.en: You are the son of Lord Sankara, the remover of obstacles, and a king with five hands. Oh Lord, please come and bless us with your compassion.

sections.label: Anupallavi
sections.ta:
அருகம்புல் கொண்டு அருமருந்தளித்த அமரா
தீங்கருகல் மோதகச் சுவை உணர்த்திய இறையே
பர்வத குமரி உடல் காப்பினின்று உதித்தவனே
தெருமுனை நின்றும் வருவினை தவிர்ப்பவனே
sections.translit:
arugampul kondu arumarundhaLittha amarA
thIngkarugal mOdhagach chuvai uNartthiya iRaiyE
parvadha kumari udal kAppinindRu udhitthavanE
therumunai nindRum varuvinai thavirppavanE
sections.en: The immortal Lord Ganesha offered the world a rare medicament using a common weed, arugampul. He revealed the delicate taste of a simple caramelized dish, modhakam. He was born from the turmeric paste on the body of Parvathi, the daughter of the mountain king Himavan. Even while standing on a street corner without shelter, He is capable of warding off the evils that may befall His devotees.

sections.label: Charanam
sections.ta:
ப்ரம்மாதி தேவர் தொழும் இறையே என்
துங்க கரி முகத்து தூமணியே
சுண்டெலி மீது ஏறி மண்டலி பைய வந்திடும் மாண்போனே
உடைந்த தந்தம் கொண்டும் உயரிய காவியம் சமைத்தவனே
சிறுமை என்று ஒன்றுமில்லை என உலகோர்க்கு
பெருமை புகட்டிய சீரே இணையடி சரணம்
sections.translit:
brahmmAdhi dhEvar thozhum iRaiyE en
thunga kari mugatthu thUmaNiyE
suNdeli mIdhu ERi maNdali paiya vandhidum mANbOnE
udaindha thandham koNdum uyariya kAviyam samaitthavanE
siRumai endRu ondRumillai ena ulagOrkku
perumai pugattiya sIrE iNaiyadi saranam
sections.en: He is the Lord of Lords, worshipped by all the gods including Brahma. He is my eminent, elephant-faced, precious pearl. This Supreme Lord moves slowly but gracefully toward the ordained altar of worship in His chariot, driven by a tiny mouse. He created the magnificent epic Mahabharata, unbelievably writing the entire text with a single broken tusk. In doing so, He taught humans that nothing in existence is small or insignificant, setting the example through His own actions. We surrender unto His incomparable feet.

notes: This piece is a medley: it opens with the viruttham “Chathur maRai nAyakan,” in praise of Ganesha as Sankari's son, before continuing into the pallavi “Sankaran maindhanE.” The anupallavi of the song incorporates several legends associated with the life of Ganesha. It extols His glory by illustrating, through examples from His own life, that nothing on earth is small or menial. One such example is the modhakam dish he relishes, which is a dumpling prepared by steaming an outer shell of rice-flour dough filled with a sweet mixture of grated coconut and jaggery, flavored with cardamom. Once, Lord Siva granted a boon to the demon Analasura, allowing him to emit fire from his eyes to ensure that no enemy could come near him. Empowered by this boon, Analasura began tormenting the celestials, who then appealed to Ganesha for help. Ganesha assumed His Visvarupam and swallowed Analasura whole. However, the demon continued to hurl fireballs from within Ganesha’s stomach, causing Him excruciating pain. Neither gentle massaging with soft flower petals nor the cooling rays of the moon brought any relief. At last, Sage Kashyapa gathered dry durva grass (Bermuda grass) and offered it to Ganesha. The moment the grass touched His stomach, the agonizing pain disappeared. Relieved, Ganesha declared that He would be pleased by devotees who offered Him a garland of arugampul and that He would bestow His blessings upon them. For more details see: Durva grass or arugampul becomes a medicine for Ganesha’s Gastric pain பிள்ளையார் புராணம், பதிப்பாசிரியர்: லேனா தமிழ்வாணன், எம்.ஏ., மணிமேகலைப் பிரசுரம், தபால் பெட்டி எண்: 1447; 4 தணிகாசலம் சாலை, தியாகராய நகர், சென்னை – 600017, மூன்றாவது பதிப்பு: 1996, பக்கம்: 162 – 165. Even the birth of Ganesha is attributed to the turmeric paste that Parvathi applied to her body during her bath. From this paste, she created a young boy and instructed him to stand guard outside her chamber so that no one could enter. When Lord Siva attempted to enter, Ganesha stopped him. Annoyed, Siva severed the boy’s head. Witnessing Parvathi’s grief and hearing the pleas of the other gods, Siva restored the boy to life by placing the head of an elephant upon his body. As atonement, he elevated Ganesha to be the chief of all the ganas—the attendants or spirits that always surround Siva—and ordained that everyone should worship Ganesha before commencing any new undertaking. Turmeric paste story The charanam of the song recounts how the great epic Mahabharata came into existence. Sage Vyasa conceived the divine tale of the Pandavas and Kauravas—the rise of enmity between the cousins, the Kurukshetra war, Krishna’s counsel to Arjuna on the battlefield, and the immense destruction that followed. Vyasa invoked Lord Brahma, who advised him to pray to Lord Ganapathy and seek His assistance as a scribe before beginning the work. Vyasa prayed to Ganesha and requested that He write down the verses at the same pace at which they were dictated. The five-handed Ganesha agreed on the condition that Vyasa should not pause or interrupt the narration. Vyasa countered with a condition of his own: that Ganesha should write only after fully understanding each verse. Recognizing the magnitude of the task, Ganesha broke off one of His tusks and used it as a quill, continuing to write tirelessly until the sacred epic was completed. The rest is history. Ganesha’s broken tusk appears in mythology, notably in the Brahmanda Purana, where He confronts Parasurama. In a fit of anger, Parasurama throws his axe—given to him by Lord Siva—at Ganesha. Rather than evade the weapon and thereby show disrespect to His father, Ganesha received the blow, which broke His tusk. Although Veda Vyasa is traditionally regarded as the author of the Brahmanda Purana, extensive research suggests that multiple authors contributed interpolations and that the text was compiled into its current form much later. It is possible that a scribe from a later puranic period merged this incident with the origin story of the Mahabharata, portraying Ganesha using His broken tusk as a writing instrument. For details see: ஶ்ரீ மஹாபாரத ஸாரம், வேதவியாசர் அருளியது, உரை ஆசிரியர் “அண்ணா”, ஶ்ரீராமகிருஷ்ண மடம், மயிலாப்பூர், சென்னை 600004, பதிப்பு 2002 பக்கம் 3. Mahabharata, C.
